ml_introduction.question: In your own words, distinguish supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, and give one real-world example of any of them.
ml_introduction.reference_answer: Supervised learning trains on labelled input-output pairs. Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data (clusters, components). Reinforcement learning learns a policy by trial-and-error rewards. Example: spam filters (supervised), customer segmentation (unsupervised), game-playing agents (RL).
rubric_points: Labels vs no labels vs reward signal distinguished (1 pt)
All three paradigms mentioned (1 pt)
Plausible real-world example (1 pt)

data_preprocessing.question: Why do we normalise or standardise features before training many ML models, and how can missing values be handled?
data_preprocessing.reference_answer: Scale-sensitive models (gradient descent, k-NN, SVM) treat large-range features as more important unless features are brought to a comparable scale. Missing values can be dropped, imputed (mean/median/mode), or modelled with an indicator.
rubric_points: Scale affecting model behaviour (1 pt)
At least one valid missing-value strategy (1 pt)
Example of a scale-sensitive method or equivalent (1 pt)

linear_regression.question: What does a linear regression coefficient mean, and name one metric used to judge fit.
linear_regression.reference_answer: A coefficient is the expected change in the target for a one-unit change in that feature, holding others fixed. Fit is judged with MSE/RMSE or R-squared.
rubric_points: Coefficient as change in target per unit feature (1 pt)
Names MSE, RMSE, or R-squared (1 pt)
Holds-other-features-fixed or similar caveat (1 pt)

logistic_regression.question: Why is logistic regression used for classification, and how do we interpret its output?
logistic_regression.reference_answer: The sigmoid squashes a linear score into a probability between 0 and 1, suitable for binary class membership. A threshold (often 0.5) converts probability to a class label; evaluation uses accuracy, precision/recall, or a confusion matrix.
rubric_points: Sigmoid / probability in [0,1] (1 pt)
Threshold to class label (1 pt)
Names a classification metric (1 pt)

decision_trees.question: How does a decision tree choose a split, and how can you reduce overfitting?
decision_trees.reference_answer: Splits maximise information gain or minimise Gini impurity. Overfitting is reduced by limiting max depth, requiring a minimum samples per leaf, or pruning.
rubric_points: Gini or entropy / information gain (1 pt)
At least one regularisation/pruning method (1 pt)
Overfitting described as fitting noise / too-deep trees (1 pt)

model_evaluation.question: Why is a train/test split (or cross-validation) necessary, and what is the difference between precision and recall?
model_evaluation.reference_answer: Evaluating on training data overestimates performance. A held-out test set or k-fold CV estimates generalisation. Precision is the fraction of predicted positives that are correct; recall is the fraction of actual positives found.
rubric_points: Need for unseen data / generalisation (1 pt)
Precision defined reasonably (1 pt)
Recall defined reasonably (1 pt)

overfitting_regularization.question: What is overfitting, and how do L1 or L2 regularisation help?
overfitting_regularization.reference_answer: Overfitting means low training error but poor generalisation. L2 (ridge) shrinks weights; L1 (lasso) can drive some weights to zero, selecting features. Both penalise complexity in the loss.
rubric_points: Train vs test gap / memorising noise (1 pt)
Penalty on weights / complexity (1 pt)
L1 vs L2 or sparsity mentioned (1 pt)

ensemble_methods.question: How do bagging and boosting differ in how they combine models?
ensemble_methods.reference_answer: Bagging trains models in parallel on bootstrap samples and averages votes (Random Forests reduce variance). Boosting trains models sequentially, each focusing on previous errors, reducing bias (e.g. AdaBoost, gradient boosting).
rubric_points: Parallel bootstrap vs sequential error-focus (1 pt)
Variance vs bias intuition or equivalent (1 pt)
Names an ensemble algorithm (1 pt)

clustering.question: What does k-means optimise, and how can you choose k?
clustering.reference_answer: k-means assigns points to the nearest of k centroids and updates centroids to minimise within-cluster squared distance. k is often chosen with the elbow method or silhouette score.
rubric_points: Centroids / within-cluster distance (1 pt)
Elbow or silhouette (or equivalent) (1 pt)
Unsupervised / no labels noted (1 pt)

neural_network_basics.question: Describe forward propagation in a feedforward network and the role of an activation function.
neural_network_basics.reference_answer: Inputs are multiplied by weights, biased, and passed through nonlinear activations layer by layer to produce an output. Activations (ReLU, sigmoid) introduce nonlinearity so the network can learn non-linear functions; weights are updated by gradient descent on a loss.
rubric_points: Weighted sum + activation through layers (1 pt)
Nonlinearity purpose (1 pt)
Learning via gradient descent / backprop mentioned (1 pt)
